video_title: AI Is Making the Market More Fragile Than Ever | Systematic Investor | Ep.420
gist: Guest Jim (with host Alan Dunne standing in for Niels) argues the bond selloff is driven by a 2026-28 refinancing wall, energy/war inflation (a Strait of Hormuz he says will stay closed), fading foreign demand and debt-funded AI capex, while S&P earnings growth is a capex-driven bubble artifact concentrated in the AI complex, making markets extremely fragile. He predicts an engineered 'V-shaped bottom': 10-year yields spiking to 5.5-6% and a 25-40% S&P drawdown, used to justify Fed long-end QE under Warsh and a US sovereign wealth fund buying equities, ending in 1960s-70s-style double-digit inflation and negative real returns. (Transcript is a garbled machine-translated auto-caption; some names and numbers are unreliable.)

insights.claim: As of September 25, the trend-following benchmark (captioned as the 'S&P Trend Index') was up about 4.45% for the month and 16% for the year, helped by predominantly short bond positioning across the long end globally and a big repricing at the short end, making 2026 one of the strongest years for trend following.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunne (host)
insights.so_what: CTA performance is heavily tied to the short-bond trend; a sharp bond reversal is the main risk to trend-follower YTD gains.

insights.claim: Nearly everyone refinanced or maxed out borrowing at near-zero rates in 2020-2021, and with a typical 5-7 year debt duration across government, corporate, private and real estate borrowers, a refinancing wall arrives in 2026-2028 at much higher rates, adding supply pressure and forcing liquidation of uneconomic investments.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Expect continued term-supply pressure and distress in leveraged assets outside AI as low-coupon debt rolls through 2028.
insights.quote: 2021 plus 5-7 years— when is that? From 2026 to 2028

insights.claim: An asset yielding 5% financed at 2.5% was profitable, but refinancing at 7.5% leaves owners choosing between negative carry or selling assets that are themselves performing poorly.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Screen for borrowers whose asset yields sit below current refinancing rates; they are forced sellers.

insights.claim: Populism leads to protectionism and then global conflict, and the resulting war in Iran is structurally inflationary because energy is the root of almost everything, with a lagged effect that compounds over time.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Treat energy-driven inflation as persistent rather than transitory; position for long-end yields to stay elevated.
insights.quote: Energy is the root of almost everything.

insights.claim: Bond buybacks and yen intervention signal that the US will ultimately print money, which raises devaluation fears and paradoxically reduces international demand for US debt, so the US is losing foreign buyers.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Watch foreign Treasury demand (auctions, TIC flows); falling foreign participation supports higher term premium.
insights.quote: Nobody wants to own American debt internationally .

insights.claim: Debt-funded AI capex, encouraged by the administration (executives pledging $600B, $400B etc. of capex by 2028 at a September 25 meeting), is creating competition for capital that pushes up yields; this shows up in credit default swaps signaling risk alongside huge borrowing demand.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler bond issuance and CDS spreads are a key gauge of the AI-capex strain on rates and credit.
insights.quote: You can call it a profit story, but in reality it is a competition for capital.

insights.claim: The two-year yield has risen roughly 90 basis points since mid-August after a CPI print closer to 0.3% than 0.2%, and markets have shifted to pricing about four rate hikes over the next year.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunne (host)
insights.so_what: Front-end repricing has been violent; hike expectations are now a crowded consensus.

insights.claim: The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen, probably for many years, despite repeated market hopes for a deal; the guest says Treasury Secretary Bessent has indicated the US will simply reroute Middle East flows.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Fade 'deal' headlines; keep structural exposure to energy and shipping disruption.
insights.quote: There is no deal. The Strait of Hormuz will not open. Probably never.

insights.claim: The guest frames the Iran war as being about control of trade and preserving the US dollar's exorbitant privilege, not about nuclear weapons or Israel.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Read US geopolitical moves through a dollar-hegemony lens to anticipate where conflict and sanctions land.
insights.quote: This is not about nuclear weapons. This is not about Israel.

insights.claim: China began trading with Iran and Venezuela in yuan, and the US moved against both countries to close that access, because losing dollar privilege is the US's Achilles heel.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Non-dollar oil trade initiatives are a leading indicator of US geopolitical escalation.
insights.quote: the US's Achilles heel is the potential loss of this enormous privilege

insights.claim: China is the main external force that could undermine the administration's control of markets and the dollar system, so investors should watch what China does as an early warning signal.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Monitor Chinese policy responses (Treasury holdings, yuan trade, retaliation) as a fragility trigger.
insights.quote: Keep an eye on China. What is China doing?

insights.claim: Rate hikes do not fix supply-side inflation; the Fed's hawkish turn is meant to strengthen the dollar and create the appearance of independence so the US can later print money at scale without looking like a banana republic.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Don't over-invest in Fed hawkishness; it may reverse sharply once a crisis justifies easing.
insights.quote: you can't look like a banana republic

insights.claim: The guest argues Warsh and the other policymaker are not truly independent of the administration, both coming from a hedge fund background and repeatedly flying on Air Force One, and the bringing of Zervos to Treasury shows hedge fund managers placed on every side of policy.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Expect coordinated Fed-Treasury action rather than an independent central bank in the next crisis.
insights.quote: a Kabuki-like project that talks about the independence of the Fed

insights.claim: The US intends to print not one trillion but tens of trillions of dollars to inject into its own economy.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Long-run debasement favors real assets over nominal bonds.
insights.quote: I'm not talking about a trillion dollars, but tens of trillions of dollars

insights.claim: Policymakers have learned to exploit mechanical strategies: they can crash markets to make trend following lose, spike volatility to force vol-target deleveraging, then reverse to squeeze flows back in, engineering V-shaped bottoms.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Systematic and vol-target strategies face policy-induced whipsaw risk; size accordingly and expect sharp reversals.
insights.quote: They can crash markets and make trend following negative.

insights.claim: The guest cites the early-2025 tariff shock (roughly a 27% drop, then a pause and reduced tariffs that squeezed the market higher) and a spring episode of escalation rhetoric followed by a 'deal' as deliberate engineered V-bottoms by hedge-fund-minded officials.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Policy-driven selloffs have been buyable; anticipate the reversal once officials pivot.
insights.quote: the V- shaped bottom is a feature. This is not a mistake.

insights.claim: Since the mid-August intervention, 10-year yields are likely at least 50bp higher, the yen has stabilized and the dollar rose against European currencies while staying stable versus the yen; an initial bond buyback announcement was quickly ignored by the market.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunne (host) / Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Small-scale buybacks have not capped yields; markets need a bigger intervention to turn.

insights.claim: The guest says de facto QE is already underway though not called that: about $9 billion of Treasury buybacks and a $60 billion yen intervention facility, with full-scale printing withheld until a worse event justifies it.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Track the size of buybacks and FX facilities as the stealth-QE dial.
insights.quote: We are currently undergoing quantitative easing. It's just that no one calls it quantitative easing.

insights.claim: This is no longer the free market of past decades but a heavily controlled one, so the most important early warning signal is politics: the administration's ability and control to keep supporting markets.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Political control (approval, legal challenges, internal cohesion) is a market risk factor to monitor.
insights.quote: Want an early warning signal? Follow politics.

insights.claim: Profit growth outside the AI complex is roughly zero or negative, per a Carlyle report the guest recommends, while bond-adjusted equity valuations are the highest ever, above the tech bubble on some metrics.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Index earnings growth is a narrow AI story; equity risk premium versus 10-year yields is at an extreme.
insights.quote: valuations have never been higher, never

insights.claim: AI-driven earnings are an artifact of the bubble: when firms like Anthropic see valuations jump from $380 billion to $2 trillion, the capital is spent on capex that becomes others' revenue and is then amortized, so the market drives profits rather than profits driving the market.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: If equity prices fall, capex and the derived earnings growth would reverse together; earnings support is reflexive, not fundamental.
insights.quote: profit does not drive the market, the market drives profit

insights.claim: Current earnings growth of around 20% is driven by bubble capex rather than AI efficiency gains, echoing 1999 when profit growth was about 27% before the bust.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Do not extrapolate current EPS growth; bubble-era earnings collapse when the funding cycle turns.
insights.quote: It literally has nothing to do with efficiency.

insights.claim: Because the market is much larger relative to the economy than in 2000, the guest estimates the economic impact of this bubble is about five times greater than the tech bubble.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: A bust would have larger macro spillovers (wealth effect, capex) than 2000-02.

insights.claim: About 45% of S&P 500 stocks have a negative beta, illustrating how market gains rest on one narrow, fragile segment.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest) / Alan Dunne (host)
insights.so_what: Index exposure is effectively a concentrated AI bet; diversification within equities is weaker than it looks.
insights.quote: 45% of the S&P have a negative beta.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler capex is about $800 billion this year and expected to exceed $1 trillion in coming years; investors should track its second and third derivatives because a slowing growth rate, not just a decline, threatens the market.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunne (host)
insights.so_what: Watch capex guidance acceleration/deceleration as the key equity signal.

insights.claim: Forecasting bubble fragility is useful even without timing, since investing is about risk-adjusted return; most investors play a '2D' up-or-down game instead of positioning for the full distribution of outcomes.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Use options and distribution-aware positioning rather than directional bets on the bubble.
insights.quote: the majority, I would say 98% of the world, still plays in a 2D world

insights.claim: The bubble persists largely because the administration backs the debt-funded buildout, with Larry Ellison described as saying firms should take on as much debt as needed because they would be bailed out; this makes the setup controlled but dependent on Trump.
insights.speaker: Alan Dunne (host)
insights.so_what: Implicit government put supports AI credit now but concentrates risk in political continuity.
insights.quote: Take on as much debt as you need, because if the worst happens, we will bail you out.

insights.claim: Like two locked tectonic plates, the absence of movement does not mean lower risk; the probability of an earthquake is rising dramatically, with Minsky-style fragility built into the system rather than a black swan.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Low realized volatility is not safety; buy convexity while it is cheap.
insights.quote: the likelihood of an earthquake or disaster is increasing dramatically

themes.theme: Engineered crash and Treasury crisis call

insights.claim: The guest predicts a V-shaped spike in 10-year Treasury yields to about 5.5-6%, happening quickly within roughly the next three months, coinciding with an equity selloff.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Specific, falsifiable rate call: position for a fast long-end blowout and correlated stock drop.
insights.quote: This would look something like 5.5-6% on 10- year bonds.

insights.claim: He expects a 25-40% S&P 500 decline, like Liberation Day, in the first two quarters of next year, with a fourth-quarter crash less likely but possible after the midterms, since the administration does not want it before them.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Tail-hedge equities into H1 next year; the window may open earlier if midterms are contested.
insights.quote: 25 to 40% in the S&P in the first two quarters of this year

insights.claim: The crash would provide the excuse to end the Fed 'Kabuki theatre' and have Warsh launch a massive long-end purchase program, foreshadowed by Hank Paulson warning months ago that a Treasury crisis was coming.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: After the spike, expect yield-curve control/QE to drive long yields sharply lower: a two-way trading opportunity.
insights.quote: There's a Treasury crisis coming .

insights.claim: Yields may run to about 6% before falling sharply to around 4% and then returning to about 5%; implied bond volatility has started rising after the 10-year broke above 5%, which the guest considers appropriate.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Long bond volatility rather than pure direction; the path is a spike-and-reversal.
insights.quote: I think it'll eventually go up to maybe 6% before it drops sharply to four

insights.claim: Equity implied volatility is still far too cheap relative to event risk around the midterms and policy; skew/asymmetry is rising but not priced in.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Buy equity downside convexity while it is underpriced.
insights.quote: it's still incredibly cheap compared to reality

insights.claim: With the House and Senate expected to swing to Democrats, the guest expects a contested midterm election (citing potential challenges to mail-in ballots), raising the chance of an earlier downturn in Q4.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Year-end becomes a riskier-than-usual window; hedge through November-December.
insights.quote: I firmly believe that this will be a contested election

themes.theme: Sovereign wealth fund and inflation endgame

insights.claim: A stock market crash would justify launching a US sovereign wealth fund, sold like Norway's $2.5 trillion fund, that prints money to buy equities on behalf of citizens (held in accounts people cannot sell), as right-wing populism competing with China's state-directed investment.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Potential state bid for strategic US equities would put a floor under 'America First' sectors after a crash.
insights.quote: It will be sold as a sovereign wealth fund, similar to Norway's sovereign wealth fund.

insights.claim: Japan already owns about 8% of the Nikkei after printing money and buying shares for 20 years, a precedent the guest says makes a US version easy to justify.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Use the BOJ ETF program as the template for how state equity buying affects markets.
insights.quote: Japan already owns 8% of the Nikkei index

insights.claim: China's solar, EV and nuclear buildouts were not driven by profit, so the free market cannot compete; the US's answer is to monetize debt and direct state capital into strategic investments.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Strategic sectors targeted by state capital are likely beneficiaries of US industrial policy.
insights.quote: How can the free market even compete with this?

insights.claim: The administration fears deflation most because the debt is unsustainable and the only exit is growth plus inflation; the guest expects an unprecedented real devaluation around late 2027 to early 2028.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Position for a second inflation wave in 2027-28: real assets, inflation hedges, short nominal duration.
insights.quote: at the end of 2027, beginning of 2028 we will see a real devaluation

insights.claim: The guest expects inflation as bad as or worse than the worst of the 1960s-70s, including double-digit rates, with real rates pushed negative as under Arthur Burns.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Nominal equity gains may mask real losses; judge returns in real terms.
insights.quote: I think you'll see inflation as bad, if not worse, than in the worst 60s and 70s.

insights.claim: Investors live in a nominal illusion: in 1962-1982 a 60/40 portfolio went nowhere and markets lost about 40% in real terms, which mirrors 1929-1949 in real terms.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: An equity rally fueled by money printing can still be a real-terms bear market.
insights.quote: we all live in a world of nominal illusions

insights.claim: 60/40's 40-year success was a function of falling rates; with inflation holding the long end up, the exit is either an equity multiple crash or massive inflation, in which stocks are the biggest risk and bonds are no hedge, so investors should diversify into strategies that profit outside stocks and bonds.
insights.speaker: Jim (guest)
insights.so_what: Allocate to alternatives (e.g., trend following, real assets) rather than relying on the stock-bond hedge.
insights.quote: Bonds are definitely not the solution for you.
